title: Arria: "Paetus, It Does Not Hurt"
text:
Pliny the Younger heard this story from Fannia, Arria's granddaughter, and wrote it down in one of his letters. He said that Arria's most famous deed was not her greatest.

Once her husband, Caecina Paetus, and their son were both seriously ill. The son died. He was a young man of rare beauty and goodness. Arria arranged the funeral so quietly that her husband did not know. Whenever she entered his room, she spoke as if their son were alive and getting better, and when he asked how the boy was, she said he had slept well and eaten with appetite. When she could no longer hold back her tears, she left the room, wept, and came back with dry eyes.

In 42 AD Paetus took part in a failed revolt against the emperor Claudius and was brought to Rome as a prisoner by ship. Arria begged to be allowed to go with him as a servant. When she was refused, she hired a small fishing boat and followed the ship. Her son-in-law Thrasea tried to persuade her not to die with her husband. To prove she was determined, she struck her head against a wall.

When Paetus was condemned to die, Arria took the dagger, plunged it into her own breast, drew it out and handed it to him, saying: "Paetus, it does not hurt."
lesson: In marriage, courage can be the gift we give each other at the worst moment. Sometimes the bravest love is the quiet kind no one sees.
people: Arria the Elder, Caecina Paetus, Fannia, Thrasea Paetus
